surfaces.part: top header band of the peg wall
pegboard front face with hung goods

answer.evidence: The board spans rows 8-46 at 32 px wide. Rows 9-13 form a cream band that brightens toward the bottom (L 169 to 249) and ends in a dark front-edge line at row 14 (L=112). That matches the 'top 5 + edge' cabinet reference. Below it the pegboard front face runs rows 15-45 (about 31 rows) with hung goods and a dark bottom outline at row 46. The yellow sign at rows 0-6 sits on top of the body, so it is decor. The top band has no distinct eave shadow, so it is a modest but valid top surface. It is borderline, since it could also be read as a front-facing header strip.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate's tile information is fine on paper: 21 visible tones per tile (references: 17 and 20 for the stall and well), and 0% near-flat coverage. The structure is shallower than the numbers suggest. All of its dark edge pixels (100%) are near-neutral, and the board frame reads as a uniform grey/black line, not a dark tone of the neighbouring material. The stall (1%) and well (33%) outlines lean brown, and the hedge (0%) leans green, so this is the sticker look. The tones come mostly from the many small coloured goods on the pegs. The board itself, a pale cream panel in a grey frame, has only about 3 lightness steps, with no grain, no plank or peg shading and no wood ramp like the stall and well. The small sign on top is also flat, with a dark outline and two or three tones. Overall it is busy but shallow in material shading, with a neutral outline. That is below the Beodeul bar.

surfaces.part: goods hanging on the peg board

answer.evidence: The main body is a 32px wide panel on rows 8-46. Rows 9-13 form a cream band that gets lighter toward the bottom and ends in a dark front-edge line at row 14 (#7a6f5a). This is the only candidate for a top surface. It could instead be a face-on header board, because no darker eave shadow follows the line (rows 15-16 are light). Rows 15-45 are the vertical peg-board face, which carries hanging goods and small peg shadows. The sign on rows 0-6 and the hung goods are decor. No side face is drawn.

styleAnswer.evidence: Measured density is fine: 21 visible tones per tile against 17 for the cheese stall and 20 for the well, with 0% near-flat coverage. The weakness is structural. 100% of the candidate's dark edge pixels are near-neutral, so the grey-black frame and outline read as a uniform sticker line. The references that carry tinted outlines (hedge 0%, cheese stall 1%, well 33%) use dark material tones instead. The cream backing panel and the frame have only about 3 lightness steps, with little per-material ramp or grain. Nearly all the richness comes from the small coloured item dots in a regular grid, not from shaded material. A careful artist would find it flatter and more sticker-like than the stall or the well, so it fails on outline and shading depth despite the tone count.

surfaces.part: top band of peg wall cabinet

answer.evidence: The body is 32px wide from row 8 to row 46. Rows 9-13 form a top band that brightens from #b5aa88 to #fffdd4. Row 13 is the lightest line and acts as the front-edge line, and row 14 (#7a6f5a) is a dark eave shadow. Below it the pegboard front face runs rows 15-45 with goods hung on it, which count as decor. The sign above the body (rows 0-6) is also decor. The top band is about 5 rows, which matches the green 'cabinet: top 5 + edge + eave' reference, so I read it as a top surface rather than a 1-2 row rim.

styleAnswer.evidence: Density holds up: 21 visible tones per tile is on par with the stall (17) and well (20), and near-flat coverage is 0%. The weakness is structural. The dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, so the frame and sign are outlined in a colourless dark grey/black line, which gives the sticker look. The Beodeul stall and well sit at 1% and 33% neutral, and the hedge at 0%, because their outlines lean toward the material. The panel's main materials (the cream backing, the grey frame and the sign) show only about 3 lightness steps each, against about 5-6 on the references. Most of the 21 tones come from the small coloured goods dotted over the pegboard, not from shaded ramps on the wall itself. The panel is a uniform grid of small items with little grain, and the wood frame has no shading. A careful artist would not accept it next to the stall and well references.

surfaces.part: top band of the peg wall
pegboard front face with hung goods

answer.evidence: The main body is a 32px-wide panel on rows 8-46. Rows 9-13 form a cream band that lightens downward (L 169 to 249) and ends in a darker front-edge line at row 14 (#7a6f5a). This meets rule (a), but it is a weak case: there are no eave shadow rows, and the band is the same cream colour as the face below. Below the line is a pegboard face of about 31 rows (15-45) with gray pegs and hung goods, each drawn with its own small top and front. The sign on rows 0-6 is decor sitting above the body. The band could also be read as a front-facing header strip, which would make this a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: Density is not the problem. The candidate has 21 visible tones per tile, against 17-20 for the stall and well, and 0% near-flat coverage, so its items and pegs give it real variety. The problem is the outline. 100% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, the same as the lamp-crook reference, while the stall, hedge and well references are tinted at 1%, 0% and 33%. The board in the image also reads as a cream panel in a dark neutral frame, which is the sticker look. The panel and frame show only about 3 lightness steps, with no per-plank grain or tinted dark-wood shading, against 5-6 steps on the stall and well wood and roof. The colourful goods supply the variety, not the material shading. Because of the near-black outline and shallow material ramps, it falls short of the Beodeul standard.
